etymology: From buy, Old English bycgan. Scripture's interest in the buyer is chiefly in what he says about the thing he is buying.
biblical_def: A buyer is a purchaser. Proverbs catches him in the act of a familiar dishonesty: “It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth” (Pro 20:14) — running down the goods to lower the price, then bragging about the bargain. Isaiah levels the market in the day of the LORD: “as with the buyer, so with the seller” (Isa 24:2). Ezekiel says of the coming judgment, “let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn” (Eze 7:12), because the property itself will not survive the change.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a buyer as one who buys; a purchaser.
webster_full: BUYER, n. One who buys; a purchaser.
scriptures: It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth.
Isa 24:2

And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him.
Eze 7:12
The time is come, the day draweth near: let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn: for wrath is upon all the multitude thereof.
Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
corruption_summary: Negotiating dishonesty is treated as skill rather than lying, and Proverbs 20:14 describes the technique so exactly that its readers usually laugh before they wince.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 20:14 is a small masterpiece of observation. It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth. Two sentences, and the whole transaction is exposed — the disparagement was never an assessment, it was a lever, and the boasting afterward proves the buyer knew the value all along. Scripture does not forbid negotiating; it forbids saying what you do not believe in order to move a price.

Ezekiel 7:12 puts every market under a longer horizon: let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn: for wrath is upon all the multitude thereof. On the eve of exile, a shrewd purchase and a forced sale come to the same thing, because the field is about to change hands regardless. That is not an argument against commerce but a caution against reading one's own cleverness in a market as evidence of God's favour.
roots_summary: Hebrew qanah (H7069), to acquire, buy — the same verb used of God acquiring His people; Greek agorazo (G59), to buy in the marketplace.
roots_lines: Hebrew qanah (H7069) — to buy, acquire, possess; Proverbs 20:14, and Exodus 15:16 of the people whom thou hast purchased.
Greek agorazo (G59) — to buy; 1 Corinthians 6:20, ye are bought with a price.
Hebrew mekher (H4242) — price, value; the object of the buyer's disparagement.
usage: “It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer” — disparagement as a lever.
“When he is gone his way, then he boasteth” — the boast proves he knew.
“Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn” — the market under judgment.

etymology: From sell, Old English sellan, to give. The seller's biblical portrait is usually of someone parting with more than the goods.
biblical_def: A seller is a vendor. Lydia is introduced as “a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God” — and the Lord opened her heart while she was about her trade (Act 16:14). Isaiah flattens the distinction in judgment: “as with the buyer, so with the seller” (Isa 24:2). Nehemiah confronts sellers who traded on the sabbath (Neh 13:20), and Christ cast out those who sold in the temple courts (Mat 21:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seller as one who sells; a vender.
webster_full: SELLER, n. One who sells; a vender.
scriptures: And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Isa 24:2

And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him.
So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice.
And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves,
corruption_summary: Commerce is treated either as spiritually irrelevant or as inherently suspect, and Lydia's conversion at her trading post refutes both.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 16:14 is quietly significant for anyone in business. A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul. She is identified by her trade, she is already a worshipper, and the Lord opens her heart in the middle of a working life. The first European convert was a merchant, and her house became the church.

Nehemiah 13 shows the other side. Merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged outside Jerusalem on the sabbath, waiting for the gates to open, and Nehemiah threatened to lay hands on them. Commerce is not condemned; commerce that will not observe a boundary is. The governor's response was to shut the gates and post Levites at them, which is a picture of what it costs to keep any commitment a market finds inconvenient.
roots_summary: Greek poleo (G4453), to sell; porphuropolis (G4211), a seller of purple — Lydia's trade, a luxury dye business.
roots_lines: Greek poleo (G4453) — to sell; Matthew 21:12, Luke 12:33, sell that ye have, and give alms.
Greek porphuropolis (G4211) — seller of purple; only Acts 16:14, of Lydia.
Hebrew makar (H4376) — to sell; Isaiah 24:2, and Genesis 37:28 of Joseph sold by his brethren.
usage: “A seller of purple… whose heart the Lord opened” — converted at her trade.
“As with the buyer, so with the seller” — judgment levels the market.
“There lodged… sellers of all kind of ware” — commerce at the sabbath gate.

etymology: The translators' rendering of the Roman denarius, using the familiar English coin. The denarius was a labourer's daily pay, which is the point in every parable that uses it.
biblical_def: A penny is the denarius, a day's wage. The householder agrees with labourers “for a penny a day” and pays the eleventh-hour men the same, provoking the complaint that shapes the parable (Mat 20:2,9–10). It is the coin brought to Christ in the tribute question: “Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny” (Mat 22:19). Two hundred pennyworth of bread would not feed the multitude (Joh 6:7), and the good Samaritan leaves two pence with the innkeeper (Luk 10:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines penny as an ancient English silver coin; and notes it is used to denote the Roman denarius in the New Testament.
webster_full: PENNY, n. An ancient English silver coin; but now an imaginary money of account, twelve of which are equal to a shilling.
2. Proverbially, a small sum.
3. Money in general.
scriptures: Mat 20:2
And when he had agreed with the labourers for a penny a day, he sent them into his vineyard.
Mat 20:9
And when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny.
Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny.
And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee.
corruption_summary: The vineyard parable is heard as a lesson about fairness in wages, when its subject is grace — and the complaint it answers is the one respectable people always make about grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 20 is precise about the arithmetic so the offence lands. The first-hour men agreed for a penny; they received a penny; nothing was withheld. Their grievance is stated exactly: thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day. Nobody was cheated — someone else was treated generously, and that was intolerable. The householder's reply is the parable's hinge: is thine eye evil, because I am good?

The tribute penny in Matthew 22 turns on an image. Whose is this image and superscription? They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's. The coin bore Caesar's image and went back to Caesar; the man asking bore God's image, and Christ leaves him to work out the implication.
roots_summary: Greek denarion (G1220), a Roman silver coin equal to a labourer's daily wage; dupsakion has no place here — the penny is always the denarius.
roots_lines: Greek denarion (G1220) — denarius, a day's wage; Matthew 20:2, 22:19, John 6:7, Revelation 6:6.
Greek assarion (G787) — farthing, a fraction of a denarius; Matthew 10:29, two sparrows sold for a farthing.
Greek lepton (G3016) — mite; Mark 12:42, the widow's two mites.
usage: “He agreed with the labourers for a penny a day” — nothing was withheld from anyone.
“Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” — the parable's hinge.
“Whose is this image and superscription?” — the coin, and the man holding it.

pos: n. (a toll or duty; also habitual practice; rendering Greek telos and ethos)
etymology: From Latin consuetudo, habit — and by extension the customary duty levied on goods. The KJV uses both senses.
biblical_def: Custom means both a levied duty and an established habit. Matthew is called from the receipt of custom (Mat 9:9), and Paul commands that dues be paid: “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom” (Rom 13:7). The other sense governs Christ's own practice: “he came to Nazareth… and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day” (Luk 4:16). Hebrews warns against forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, “as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines custom as frequent or common use, habitual practice; and as tribute, toll or tax, the duties imposed on goods.
webster_full: CUSTOM, n. Frequent or common use, or practice; a frequent repetition of the same act; habitual practice.
2. A buying of goods; practice of frequenting a shop and purchasing.
3. Tribute, toll or tax; that is, cost or charge paid to the public.
scriptures: Mat 9:9
And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.
Rom 13:7
Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
Luk 4:16
And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: Habit is dismissed as dead routine by people whose devotion collapses without it — while Luke records that gathered worship was Christ's own settled custom.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 4:16 contains four words that answer a long modern argument: as his custom was. The Son of God, who needed no instruction and had nothing to learn from the reader in the Nazareth synagogue, attended weekly by habit. The passage is not about the quality of that synagogue — the congregation tried to kill Him before the day was out. It is about a practice maintained regardless, which is what a custom is.

Romans 13:7 keeps the other sense from being spiritualized away. Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour. Paying customs duties honestly is placed in the same sentence as honour and fear, which means a believer's tax return belongs to his discipleship and not merely to his accounting.
roots_summary: Greek telos (G5056), a toll or custom duty; telonion (G5058), the tax booth; ethos (G1485), a habit or established usage.
roots_lines: Greek telos (G5056) — custom, toll; Matthew 17:25, Romans 13:7.
Greek telonion (G5058) — the receipt of custom, tax booth; Matthew 9:9, Mark 2:14.
Greek ethos (G1485) — custom, habit; Luke 4:16, 22:39, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives.
usage: “Sitting at the receipt of custom” — where Matthew was called.
“Custom to whom custom” — duties paid as discipleship.
“As his custom was, he went into the synagogue” — habit that needed no inspiration.

etymology: From Italian traffico, trade. The KJV spelling with a final k preserves the older form; the word means commerce, without the modern criminal connotation.
biblical_def: Traffick is trade. Ezekiel's lament over Tyre is the great passage: the city is addressed as one whose “traffick” filled her with violence, and the charge against her king is theological — “by the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned” (Eze 28:16). Joseph's brothers are told to traffick in the land (Gen 42:34), and Solomon's wealth came partly “of the traffick of the spice merchants” (1Ki 10:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines traffic as trade, commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling; and commodities of trade.
webster_full: TRAFFIC, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling.
2. Commodities of trade.
TRAFFIC, v.i. To trade; to pass goods and commodities from one person to another for an equivalent.
scriptures: By the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned: therefore I will cast thee as profane out of the mountain of God: and I will destroy thee, O covering cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire.
And bring your youngest brother unto me: then shall I know that ye are no spies, but that ye are true men: so will I deliver you your brother, and ye shall traffick in the land.
Beside that he had of the merchantmen, and of the traffick of the spice merchants, and of all the kings of Arabia, and of the governors of the country.
Eze 28:5
By thy great wisdom and by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches, and thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches:
corruption_summary: Trade is defended or denounced wholesale, while Ezekiel makes a finer charge — that a particular commercial success bred violence and a settled belief in one's own divinity.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 28 traces a specific sequence, and it is worth following. By thy great wisdom and by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches, and thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches. Skill produced wealth; wealth produced pride; pride produced the claim I am a God, I sit in the seat of God. Nothing in the chain is inevitable, but each step is ordinary, and Tyre's merchants would have described every stage as success.

The verdict names the mechanism: by the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence. Scale is the aggravating factor. A trade conducted at volume develops a distance between the transaction and its human cost, and the violence arrives in the middle of the city without anyone deciding to be violent. That is a warning any prosperous economy can read directly.
roots_summary: Hebrew rekullah (H7404), traffic, merchandise; sachar (H5503), to travel about as a trader — the merchant is a goer-about.
roots_lines: Hebrew rekullah (H7404) — traffic, merchandise; Ezekiel 26:12, 28:5, 16, 18.
Hebrew sachar (H5503) — to trade, travel about; Genesis 42:34, ye shall traffick in the land.
Hebrew maarab (H4627) — merchandise, wares; the cargo lists of Ezekiel 27.
usage: “By thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches” — skill, then wealth, then pride.
“Filled the midst of thee with violence” — volume creates distance from cost.
“Ye shall traffick in the land” — ordinary trade, permitted.

pos: n. (a plumb line's weight; rendering Hebrew mishqeleth and anak)
etymology: From Latin plumbum, lead. A plummet is a lead weight on a cord — the simplest possible test of true vertical, and one that cannot be argued with.
biblical_def: A plummet is the weight of a plumb line. God announces judgment on Jerusalem by it: “I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab” (2Ki 21:13). Amos sees the LORD standing on a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in His hand: “Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel” (Amo 7:7–8). Isaiah promises the opposite use, laying a foundation stone and setting “judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet” (Isa 28:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plummet as a long piece of lead attached to a line, used in sounding the depth of water; and an instrument used by carpenters and masons to determine a perpendicular.
webster_full: PLUMMET, n. A long piece of lead attached to a line, used in sounding the depth of water.
2. An instrument used by carpenters, masons, etc. in adjusting erections to a perpendicular line.
3. Any weight.
scriptures: Amo 7:7
Thus he shewed me: and, behold, the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand.
Amo 7:8
And the LORD said unto me, Amos, what seest thou? And I said, A plumbline. Then said the Lord, Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more:
Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place.
And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down.
corruption_summary: Standards are argued as preferences, which is only possible where no plumbline is admitted — and a wall with no vertical reference can lean a long way while looking fine from inside.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 7 is a vision of measurement rather than of violence. The LORD stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand… Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more. Nothing is struck in the vision; a standard is simply applied. That is the terror of it — the wall does not have to be attacked, only measured, and the lean it has been living with becomes undeniable.

The plumbline's authority comes from outside the building. It hangs by gravity, indifferent to the mason's intentions, the wall's history, or how straight it looks to those inside. Every generation prefers to assess itself by comparison with the wall next door, which is why Isaiah's promise is so pointed: judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet. God builds with an external reference.
roots_summary: Hebrew anak (H594), a plumbline or lead; mishqeleth (H4949), a levelling weight; both occur only in these judgment passages.
roots_lines: Hebrew anak (H594) — plumbline; only Amos 7:7-8, four occurrences.
Hebrew mishqeleth (H4949) — plummet, level; 2 Kings 21:13, Isaiah 28:17.
Hebrew qav (H6957) — measuring line; the companion instrument, judgment laid to the line.
usage: “I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel” — measured, not attacked.
“Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet” — God builds true.
“The plummet of the house of Ahab” — measured against a known ruin.

pos: n., v. (a trade of one thing for another; rendering Greek antallagma)
etymology: From Latin excambiare, to barter. An exchange assumes both parties value what they receive above what they give — which is exactly what Christ's use interrogates.
biblical_def: An exchange is a trade. Christ's question makes it the most serious word in commerce: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?” (Mat 16:26). Job says of wisdom that “the exchange of it shall not be for jewels of fine gold” (Job 28:17). The law forbids exchanging a devoted animal for another (Lev 27:10), and Ezekiel's land-portion may not be exchanged away (Eze 48:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exchange as in commerce, the act of giving one thing or commodity for another; barter; and the thing given in return.
webster_full: EXCHANGE, v.t. To give one thing or commodity for another; to alienate or transfer the property of a thing and receive in compensation for it something of supposed equal value.
EXCHANGE, n. In commerce, the act of giving one thing or commodity for another; barter.
2. The thing given in return for something received.
scriptures: For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?
The gold and the crystal cannot equal it: and the exchange of it shall not be for jewels of fine gold.
He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change beast for beast, then it and the exchange thereof shall be holy.
Mar 8:37
Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?
corruption_summary: Every culture prices souls implicitly — by what people trade their lives for — and Christ's question simply makes the transaction explicit enough to see.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 16:26 works as an accounting problem. Gain the whole world is set as the maximum possible return, and lose his own soul as the cost, and Christ asks whether the trade profits. The second half is the harder question: what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? — because it asks after the buy-back price. Once traded, there is no asset left with which to repurchase it. The transaction is one-way, which is what makes it worth interrogating in advance.

Job 28 is the passage that supplies the vocabulary for pricing what cannot be priced. It cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof… the exchange of it shall not be for jewels of fine gold. Wisdom sits outside the market, and the chapter ends by locating it: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding. What cannot be bought can still be received.
roots_summary: Greek antallagma (G465), an exchange, the price paid in return; Hebrew temurah (H8545), exchange or substitution, the word of Leviticus 27:10.
roots_lines: Greek antallagma (G465) — that which is given in exchange; Matthew 16:26, Mark 8:37.
Hebrew temurah (H8545) — exchange, substitution; Leviticus 27:10, 33, Job 28:17, Ruth 4:7.
Hebrew machiyr (H4242) — price; Job 28:15, it cannot be gotten for gold.
usage: “What shall a man give in exchange for his soul?” — the buy-back question.
“The exchange of it shall not be for jewels of fine gold” — wisdom sits outside the market.
“He shall not alter it, nor change it” — the devoted thing is not tradeable.

pos: n. (a levy on passage or goods; rendering Aramaic halak)
etymology: From Greek telos through Old English, a tax. A toll is charged for passage — a levy on movement rather than on production.
biblical_def: A toll is a levy. Ezra records a Persian decree exempting the temple's servants from it: “it shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them” — upon priests, Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, and ministers of the house of God (Ezr 7:24). The adversaries of the rebuilding had earlier warned Artaxerxes that a restored Jerusalem would not pay “toll, tribute, and custom” (Ezr 4:13), and the work was stopped on that argument.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines toll as a tax paid for some liberty or privilege, particularly for passage over a bridge or on a highway; and a portion of grain taken by a miller for grinding.
webster_full: TOLL, n. A tax paid for some liberty or privilege, particularly for the privilege of passing over a bridge or on a highway.
2. A liberty to buy and sell within the bounds of a manor.
3. A portion of grain taken by a miller as a compensation for grinding.
scriptures: Ezr 7:24

Also we certify you, that touching any of the priests and Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, or ministers of this house of God, it shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them.
Ezr 4:13
Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.
Ezr 4:21
Give ye now commandment to cause these men to cease, and that this city be not builded, until another commandment shall be given from me. Give: Chaldee, Make a decree

He saith, Yes. And when he was come into the house, Jesus prevented him, saying, What thinkest thou, Simon? of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? of their own children, or of strangers?
corruption_summary: Religious tax exemption is defended as a right where Ezra records it as a king's gift — granted by pagan power, and therefore revocable by it.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 7:24 is remarkable for its source. A Persian king exempts the whole temple staff from toll, tribute, and custom — a concession that no Israelite had the power to demand. Artaxerxes grants it because he fears the wrath of the God of heaven, and the exemption exists at his pleasure. Any church that treats such privileges as inalienable rights rather than as providential gifts has forgotten how they were obtained.

Ezra 4:13 shows the other edge. Adversaries wrote to the king warning that if this city be builded… then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings — and the work stopped. The accusation that a religious community is a fiscal liability is very old, it was effective, and it is answered less by argument than by the conduct Christ prescribed when He paid the temple tax lest we should offend them.
roots_summary: Aramaic halak (H1983), toll or road-tax, in the Aramaic sections of Ezra; joined with middah, tribute, and belo, custom.
roots_lines: Aramaic halak (H1983) — toll, road tax; Ezra 4:13, 20, 7:24.
Aramaic middah (H4061) — tribute; the companion levy in the same verses.
Greek telos (G5056) — custom, toll; Matthew 17:25, of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute?
usage: “It shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them” — a pagan king's grant.
“Then will they not pay toll… and so thou shalt endamage the revenue” — the old accusation.
“Lest we should offend them” — Christ pays anyway.

pos: n. (a weight, a sum of money; rendering Greek mna and litra)
etymology: From Latin pondo, by weight. In Luke the pound is the Greek mna, about three months' wages; in John it is the litra, a weight of about twelve ounces.
biblical_def: A pound is a weight or a sum. Christ's parable of the pounds gives every servant the same amount — “he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come” (Luk 19:13) — and rewards them by return: the man whose pound gained ten receives authority over ten cities. Mary anoints Christ with “a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly” (Joh 12:3), and Nicodemus brings myrrh and aloes “about an hundred pound weight” (Joh 19:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pound as a standard weight consisting of twelve ounces troy or sixteen ounces avoirdupois; and a money of account consisting of twenty shillings.
webster_full: POUND, n. A standard weight consisting of twelve ounces troy, or sixteen ounces avoirdupois.
2. A money of account consisting of twenty shillings.
POUND, n. An inclosure erected by authority, in which cattle or other beasts are confined.
scriptures: And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come.
And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.
Joh 12:3
Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment.
And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight.
corruption_summary: The parable of the pounds differs from the talents precisely where the church usually blurs them — here every servant receives the same, so the difference in outcome is entirely faithfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke's parable removes the excuse that Matthew's leaves available. In the talents, the servants receive five, two, and one, according to their several ability; in the pounds, ten servants receive one pound each. Identical stock, identical instruction — occupy till I come — and radically different returns. The variable is not gifting but use, which is why the unprofitable servant's defence collapses into a description of his own view of the master: I feared thee, because thou art an austere man.

The reward structure is also worth noting: the man who gained ten pounds receives authority over ten cities. The return is not more money but more responsibility, in a kingdom. Faithfulness in a very little is treated as the qualification for governing, which reorders how a Christian should think about small unnoticed obedience in the present.
roots_summary: Greek mna (G3414), a mina, about a hundred denarii; litra (G3046), a Roman pound of about twelve ounces — two different words, both rendered pound.
roots_lines: Greek mna (G3414) — mina, pound of money; Luke 19:13-25.
Greek litra (G3046) — a pound weight; John 12:3, 19:39.
Greek pragmateuomai (G4231) — to trade, occupy; Luke 19:13, occupy till I come.
usage: “Delivered them ten pounds… Occupy till I come” — identical stock, different returns.
“Have thou authority over ten cities” — the reward is responsibility.
“A pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly” — the weight Mary poured out.

pos: v. (to determine weight, to consider; rendering Hebrew shaqal and takan)
etymology: Old English wegan, to carry or balance. The same verb serves for scales and for judgment, which is Scripture's whole point.
biblical_def: To weigh is to test by balance. Hannah's song announces that “by him actions are weighed” (1Sa 2:3). Job asks to be measured honestly: “Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity” (Job 31:6). Belshazzar reads his sentence in the same figure: “TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting” (Dan 5:27). Proverbs adds that a man's own estimate is not the reading that counts: “all the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits” (Pro 16:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines weigh as to examine by the balance; to ascertain the weight; and to pay, allot or take by weight; also to consider, to examine in the mind.
webster_full: WEIGH, v.t. To examine by the balance; to ascertain the weight, that is, the force with which a thing tends to the center of gravity.
2. To be equivalent to in weight.
3. To pay, allot or take by weight.
4. To consider; to deliberate upon; to examine for the purpose of forming an opinion.
scriptures: Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.
Job 31:6
Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity.
Dan 5:27
TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.
Pro 16:2
All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits.
corruption_summary: Self-assessment has become the final court, and Proverbs 16:2 states the exact flaw — a man's ways are always clean in his own eyes, which is why his eyes are not the scale.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 16:2 is the verse that dismantles the modern conscience's confidence in itself. All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits. It does not say some men rationalize; it says the internal verdict is reliably favourable, which makes it useless as evidence. That is not a counsel of despair but of humility: the reading that matters is taken on a scale we do not hold.

Daniel 5:27 shows the reading given. TEKEL is a weight-word, and the interpretation is one sentence long: Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting. Belshazzar had a kingdom, a feast, and a thousand lords, and none of it registered. The chapter's detail is worth keeping — he knew his father's story, and humbled not his heart, though he knew all this. What was wanting was not information.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaqal (H8254), to weigh out — the root of shekel; takan (H8505), to measure or weigh; Aramaic teqal, the TEKEL of Daniel 5.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaqal (H8254) — to weigh; Job 31:6, Isaiah 40:12, weighed the mountains in scales.
Hebrew takan (H8505) — to weigh, measure, ponder; 1 Samuel 2:3, Proverbs 16:2, the LORD weigheth the spirits.
Aramaic teqal (H8625) — to weigh; Daniel 5:27, thou art weighed in the balances.
usage: “By him actions are weighed” — Hannah's song names the scale.
“Let me be weighed in an even balance” — Job asks for honest measurement.
“The LORD weigheth the spirits” — the internal verdict is not the reading.
